title: Posterior calibration
dek: A posterior is calibrated if, among the days you quoted 80% intervals, about 80% of those intervals cover the thing you claimed. Computation plus a prior does not grant this for free.
story: Bayesian computation produces numbers. Calibration asks whether those numbers match frequencies in a world you are willing to describe. If you simulate θ from a prior (or from a hierarchical hyperprior), then y from the likelihood, then form 90% credible intervals, about 90% should cover θ — for that data-generating process.

If the likelihood omitted clustering, intervals will be too short. If the prior was wildly concentrated, they will cover the prior’s favourite neighbourhood, not the lab’s. Posterior predictive checks (replicate y_rep from p(y_rep | y) and compare to y) catch some of this without needing the true θ.

A 95% credible interval is still not a 95% confidence interval. You can have approximate frequentist coverage as a bonus of a well-specified model and a not-insane prior. You cannot rename the bonus as the definition.
deepTitle: PPC, PIT, and simulation from the joint
deep: Posterior predictive: y_rep ~ p(y_rep | y) = ∫ f(y_rep | θ) p(θ | y) dθ. Histograms of a discrepancy T(y_rep) versus T(y_obs) are a visual test. If T is the number of zeros in weekly counts and y_obs has far more zeros than y_rep, the Poisson-without-mixture story failed.

Probability integral transform: if the predictive cdf is right, F(y_obs | past) should look Uniform. Used more in sequential forecasting than in a one-shot DST paper, but the idea is the same: probabilities should be frequencies of events you defined.

Hierarchical calibration is trickier: you may want calibration for district-level θⱼ, not only for the hypermean μ. Shrinking hard can be well-calibrated for μ and poorly calibrated for a particular referral hospital that was never exchangeable.
MCMC error is not miscalibration of the model; it is miscomputation. Mixing the two in a diagnostics paragraph is how people “fix” a wrong likelihood by running more iterations.

formulas.label: Posterior predictive
formulas.expression: p(y_rep | y) = ∫ f(y_rep | θ) p(θ | y) dθ
formulas.note: Compare T(y_rep) to T(y). That is a check of the joint model, prior included.

formulas.label: Nominal coverage (simulation)
formulas.note: A property you can measure in fake-data simulation. Not automatic.

visual.caption: Schematic calibration of 80% credible intervals under three DGPs: well-specified iid Bernoulli, same mean with ignored household clustering, and a prior piled at the wrong end of π. Only the first bar sits near 80.

example.title: Too-short intervals on district FQ-R
example.setup: Beta-Binomial iid model on isolates, 80% posterior intervals for each district’s πⱼ. A fake-data study that includes household clustering shows ~55% coverage.

steps.title: The PPC hint
steps.body: T = variance of district-level ȳⱼ. y_rep from the iid Beta-Binomial is too homogeneous. The data’s T sits in the tail of T(y_rep).

steps.title: Repair the likelihood
steps.body: Add a district or household random effect, or a Dirichlet-multinomial. Re-simulate coverage. The prior on τ now matters for unit-level calibration.

steps.title: Do not lengthen intervals by hand
steps.body: Multiplying SDs by 1.5 in a figure is not a posterior. If you need a conservative interval for policy, say so as a decision rule, not as p(π | y).

example.takeaway: Calibration is a property of the whole joint model under a DGP you name. Credible is not a synonym for covered.

check.prompt: A 90% credible interval is guaranteed to have 90% frequentist coverage:
choices: Only under extra conditions (model and prior matching the DGP, regularity, honest computation) — not by the word “credible”
check.answer: Only under extra conditions (model and prior matching the DGP, regularity, honest computation) — not by the word “credible”
check.why: Definition is posterior probability. Coverage is a sampling property you can check.

whyWrong.Always, by Bayes’ theorem: Bayes gives p(θ|y), not automatic coverage.

check.prompt: You simulated 200 fake datasets from a DGP and built 80% credible intervals. 110 covered the true θ. Estimated coverage is:
check.why: 110/200 = 0.55. Nominal was 80; this DGP is miscalibrated (too short or off-centre).

check.prompt: On the calibration small-multiples, the short cover% bar under “ignored clusters” is claiming:
choices: An iid posterior that pretends isolates are independent will typically undercover θ when the DGP is clustered
check.answer: An iid posterior that pretends isolates are independent will typically undercover θ when the DGP is clustered
check.why: Fake precision. Same lesson as sandwich and mixed models, now in a Bayesian caption.

whyWrong.Clustering makes intervals too wide: The bar is short: undercoverage, too tight.
whyWrong.Priors cannot affect coverage: The third panel is exactly that.
whyWrong.80% is a p-value: It is a nominal interval level.
